# The Last Thing in Lost Property

The last thing anyone came to claim was a door.

“A door to what?” I asked.

The girl considered this. “That depends which way you’re going.”

She was fourteen, perhaps fifteen, and had arrived on the last afternoon of the municipal lost-property office with a canvas shopping bag and a claim ticket on which someone had written, in pencil, BIG FLAT THING. This was typical of our drivers. One of them had once handed in a cello as POSSIBLE GUITAR. For three weeks, its owner and I had been victims of the word *possible*.

“Was it lost on a bus?”

“On the forty-six.”

“Was it attached to the bus?”

“No.”

I asked the second question out of habit. We had rules about fixtures.

Behind me, the shelves were bare except for a pair of yellow swimming fins and a lunch box that smelled, even after six months, astonishingly of oranges. Everything else had been collected, donated, or put on the truck for the depot across town. At five, I was to leave my keys in an envelope on the desk. On Monday, a man named Craig would come to measure the room for a coffee franchise. I knew his name because he had already come once, two weeks early, and asked me whether the floor was level.

“It was when I started,” I told him.

The girl gave me the ticket. On the back was the number of the bus and, in the upper corner, a little drawing of a fish.

“That’s my fish,” she said. “In case you were wondering.”

“I was wondering about the door.”

“Oh. It’s green.”

There was a green door in the office. It was behind the filing cabinet, where we had put it after discovering that a door leaning against a wall invites people to open it. Two visitors had tried. The second had looked at the handle in his hand as if it had betrayed him personally.

I led the girl around the counter.

“Is that it?”

She put her palm on the green paint. “I need to see underneath.”

Together we pulled the door out. It was heavier than I remembered. A strip of brown felt had been glued along one edge, and there was a dent near the lock, exactly the right size to have been made by the back of a spoon. On the unpainted side, written in pencil, were the words:

*Fifty people: six onions unless Mrs. N. is coming.*

The girl crouched down.

“That’s it,” she said. “Mrs. N. is my grandmother.”

“Does she like onions?”

“She brings her own. She thinks no one else cooks them long enough.”

Below the onions were other pencilled notes, some in English, some in a language I didn’t recognize. A line of arithmetic ended in a small, angry cloud. Someone had drawn the outline of a hand and written *JUNE 2019* inside it. The girl put her hand over the drawing. The fingers of the drawing stuck out past hers.

“That’s my brother’s,” she said. “He was twelve. Disgusting, really, how fast he grew.”

I got a release form.

“Name of owner?”

“Everybody.”

“I’ll need a name I can put on the form.”

“Put my grandmother.”

“Did she own it?”

The girl thought awhile. “She paid for the hinges.”

I had a supervisor I could call. She had told me that if there were any unresolved claims on the final day, I should call. She had also told me that her son was going to read a poem at school at four, the first time he had agreed to speak in front of anybody since Christmas. It was four twelve. Whatever the proper disposition of the door, there was no need to involve a boy reading a poem.

“Where are you taking it?” I asked.

“Number eight, Larch Street.”

I knew the building. The ground floor had been a laundrette, then a shop that sold phones and repaired shoes, sometimes in the same transaction. The upper floors had balconies just deep enough to stand on if you didn’t mind your toes sticking through the railings.

“How did it get on the bus in the first place?”

“With difficulty,” she said.

She looked at me to see if I would let her get away with that. When I didn’t say anything, she sat on the edge of the counter and told me.

The door had come off the old boiler room in the basement of number eight. For eleven years it had lain across two trestles on Thursday evenings. Dinner had started with three women waiting for their washing to finish and ended up feeding anybody who turned up at seven. In warm weather they carried the door into the yard. Renters came and went, and some of them still returned on Thursdays, even after they had moved farther away than you would think anyone would travel for lentils.

Then the building changed hands. The new owners found water coming in behind the basement wall, and while the repairs were being done, the room had to be cleared. A man in an orange vest pointed to a skip and told the girl’s brother, who had come to help his grandmother, that anything nobody wanted should go in there.

“He thought the man was going to throw it out himself,” the girl said. “So he took it.”

“Where was he going?”

“To our uncle’s. He has a shed.”

“How do you accidentally leave a door on a bus?”

“You get off at the front to ask the driver to open the back. He doesn’t understand you because you’ve put your earphones in your pocket without turning the music off, and you think he’s saying yes when actually he’s saying stand clear.”

I laughed. The girl didn’t.

“He went all the way to the terminus after it. Then he told Gran he’d got it into the shed. He’s been going over to our uncle’s every Thursday for a month so she’ll think he’s checking on it.”

“Does your uncle know?”

“My uncle thinks he’s finally taking an interest in him.”

I laughed again, and this time she did too, though she tried to disguise it as a cough.

The door had arrived from the terminus on Tuesday. Until then it had been propped against a vending machine with a handwritten sign reading OUT OF ORDER. Quite a lot of lost property was not lost in the interesting sense. It was six feet away, being mistaken for a sign.

I put the form down between us.

“If I put your name, will you sign for it?”

“Yes.”

“Can you carry it?”

“Yes,” she said, without the same conviction.

She opened her shopping bag. It contained a skein of thin blue rope, a folded dish towel, and two apples. One apple had a bite out of it. She took it out, examined the bite as if it might have happened in transit, and took another.

Her name was Leila. She signed with a tiny, tidy signature that looked nothing like the fish.

We tried the rope first. The idea, as I understood it, was to make a kind of shoulder strap. With the door upright, Leila managed three steps before it swung outward and knocked the fins off the shelf. We tried putting the towel between the rope and her shoulder. This helped her shoulder but did nothing for the fins.

“We could get the forty-six,” she said.

I looked at her.

“Yes,” she said. “I know.”

I had a small cart in the cupboard, a folding thing with red wheels that I used for boxes of paper. It belonged to me, though it had been in the office long enough to acquire a municipal sticker and a dent made by someone who had never admitted borrowing it. If we laid the door on the cart and tied it down, one of us could hold each end. Larch Street was less than a mile away.

I looked at the clock. Four thirty-eight.

When I first took the job, my husband used to meet me at five and we would walk to the market. He liked to stand at the fish counter asking questions he already knew the answers to. “What would you do with these?” he would ask, pointing to the sardines, and the fishmonger, who knew perfectly well what he would do with them because he had told him every Friday for eight years, would explain again about the lemon and the salt.

After he died, I worked late on Fridays. There was no practical reason for it. At five the buses made one kind of noise outside the office, and at six they made another; by staying late I could leave to the wrong noise.

I’d intended to work late on this last Friday too. I had even left myself a drawer to clear. It contained a spare cardigan and some stamps. I could have emptied it in nine seconds.

“Get the other end,” I told Leila.

We laid the door green side down on the cart and passed the rope under it twice. I unplugged the kettle, put the stamps in my pocket, and carried the cardigan out under my arm. After a week of saying goodbye to people who had been coming in for years, I had thought there would be something left to do at the office itself. There wasn’t. The municipal envelope had a window too low for the address printed on the sheet inside. I adjusted the sheet, put the keys in, and left it on the desk.

Outside, Leila took the front end of the door and set off faster than I could comfortably walk.

“Have you told anybody we’re coming?”

“No.”

“Do we have somewhere to put it?”

She didn’t answer.

At the crossing, a man eating chips from a paper carton asked if we’d install it for him.

“Depends what you’re paying,” Leila said.

He offered a chip. She accepted, so he gave me one too. The light changed before he had time to put vinegar on either of them.

Halfway down Larch Street we lost one of the wheels. It came off on a slope and rolled back past us in a leisurely way, as if reconsidering its destination. Leila ran after it. I stood with the door tilted against my hip, trying not to scrape it along the pavement, while a woman watering the plants outside a hairdresser’s watched me from across the street.

“Is that the table?” the woman called.

“It’s a door,” I called back.

“Yes, I know it’s a door. Is it the table?”

The woman put down her watering can. Her name was Denise, and she had done hair on Larch Street for twenty-three years. She fetched a pair of pliers, a bent nail, and a man named Louis, who had been waiting for his daughter to finish getting her hair braided. Louis knelt on the pavement and repaired the axle while Leila stood with both arms around the end of the door.

“I thought you’d all finished with that,” Denise said.

“We were waiting for the room,” Leila said.

“It’s finished. They’ve got exercise bikes in it now.”

Leila looked at her.

“Only three,” Denise added, as though the number might help.

Louis spun the wheel. It wobbled but stayed on.

We didn’t go any farther for a minute. I could see the balconies of number eight from where we stood. Someone had hung a white shirt over one of the railings. Its sleeves kept lifting in the wind.

“Your gran hasn’t been down there, then,” Denise said.

“She has,” said Leila. “She’s been three times. She told me the workmen must be having trouble with the floor.”

Denise picked up her watering can and took it inside. When she came back, she had a plastic chair, which she set on the pavement. None of us sat in it.

“My brother’s in the shed now,” Leila said. She was looking at her phone. “He says our uncle’s showing him how to sharpen a pair of shears.”

“Tell him we’ve got the door,” I said.

“He’ll want to know where to take it.”

“Tell him where it is.”

She typed with both thumbs. Then she looked up at Denise.

“Does your water come out hot enough to wash dishes?”

“Hot enough to remove skin,” Denise said. “Why?”

Leila bent over the door to loosen the rope. “I’m calling my gran.”

That first Friday dinner nobody cooked. This has been disputed since, chiefly by Denise, who says that buying a hot chicken and cutting it into eight uneven pieces constitutes cooking. Louis brought the trestles from the cupboard under his stairs, where they had been all along. The woman from the corner shop brought paper plates and stood at the end of the table explaining that she couldn’t stay, right up until somebody took her coat.

Leila’s brother arrived with their uncle, who was carrying a pair of freshly sharpened shears. Their grandmother arrived last. She carried a jar of onions and a bottle of washing-up liquid in a bag that also contained, for reasons she never explained, a single clean sock.

Leila’s brother looked at his grandmother and began, “I can explain.”

“I should hope so,” she said. “I’ve been paying your uncle five pounds a week to keep you out of that shed.”

Their uncle put the shears down. The boy looked from one to the other, and it wasn’t until both of them laughed that I realized they were lying, and not particularly well.

We set the door green side up. There was a brisk discussion about whether it could stay in the hairdresser’s overnight. It couldn’t: Denise had a wedding party at nine and needed all her floor. Louis offered his hallway, provided it was gone before his daughter’s bicycle came out in the morning. Nobody knew where it would go after that. Leila put a paper plate over the hole where the handle had been.

I sat down when the chair became free. Somebody had brought sardines, the cheap kind in a tin, and I pulled back the lid and put a few on my plate. Leila passed me a lemon half without my asking. I squeezed it hard enough to get a seed in my eye. For a minute I could see nothing on that side but a bright, watery blur, and when it cleared everyone was still there, reaching over one another for bread.

A few weeks later I went past the old office. The floor, it turned out, was not level. Craig had solved this by raising one end of the counter, and now the little glass case full of pastries stood exactly where our shelf of ownerless umbrellas had been. I bought a coffee. It was good. I had been hoping it wouldn’t be.

The door acquires a new address every so often. It spends most weeks, at present, standing on edge in Louis’s hallway. His daughter has learned to wheel her bicycle past it without catching the pedals, though not without complaining. There is talk of asking the new owners for the basement on Friday evenings, since nobody has ever seen all three exercise bikes in use at once. There is also talk of staying on the pavement until the weather makes us stop. People get up from dinner and go to the bus stop, and people coming home on the bus see us and sit down.

Last Friday I arrived early. Leila was there, rubbing at a blot of candle wax with her thumbnail. She had a pencil tucked behind her ear. I asked if she needed it for school.

“No,” she said. “Turn this over with me a second.”

We tipped the door up off the trestles. The old notes were still there, darker in some places from the grease that had worked its way into the wood. Leila found a space alongside the angry cloud, took the pencil from behind her ear, and wrote *If raining, ask Denise*.

Then she squatted down and added, smaller, *Ask nicely*.

The moral emphasis is on making room for one another through modest, collective acts rather than formal ownership or perfect plans.

Medium — The sustained, distinctive use of ordinary objects to connect grief with communal care makes this a strong signal within the sample.
